We can also factor constants outside of an expected value expression. So for any constant [MATH: a] and any random variable [MATH: X,] we have

Content:
[MATH: \textrm E[aX] = a \textrm E[X].]

Content:

Content:

A random variable [MATH: X] has the probability distribution given below.

| [MATH: x] | [MATH: 0] | [MATH: 1] | [MATH: 2] | [MATH: 3] | [MATH: 4] |
| [MATH: f(x)] | [MATH: \dfrac{1}{5}] | [MATH: \dfrac{1}{10}] | [MATH: \dfrac{3}{10}] | [MATH: \dfrac{3}{10}] | [MATH: \dfrac{1}{10}] |

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
First, let's find [MATH: \textrm E[X].]

The expected value of a discrete random variable [MATH: X] with probability mass function [MATH: f(x)] and sample space [MATH: S] is given by

[MATH: \textrm E[X] = \sum\limits_{x \in S} x \cdot f(x).]

Summing up the products of each value of [MATH: X] and its associated probability, we get

[MATH: E[X]|= ∑_(x ∈ S)x ⋅ f(x); = 0 ⋅ (1)/(5) + 1 ⋅ (1)/(10) + 2 ⋅ (3)/(10) + 3 ⋅ (3)/(10) + 4 ⋅ (1)/(10); = 2.]

Therefore,

[MATH: E[(1)/(4)X]|= E[(1)/(4)X]; = (1)/(4)E[X]; = (1)/(4) ⋅ 2; = (1)/(2).]

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
There are several important properties that we can use to simplify expressions involving expected values.

Content:
The first property is that the expected value of a constant is just the constant itself. That is, for any constant [MATH: a,] we have
[MATH: \textrm E[a] = a.]

Content:
For example,

Content:
[MATH: \textrm E[5] = 5,\qquad \textrm E[-99] = -99,\qquad \textrm E[\sqrt 2] = \sqrt 2.]

Content:
The idea that the expected value of a constant is equal to the same constant makes intuitive sense. If [MATH: a] is a constant, then it does not vary. Therefore, it is always sure to have the same value.

---

Item 2 — Example: Computing the Expected Value of a Constant

Example Prompt:
Compute [MATH: \textrm E[1.2].]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
For any constant [MATH: a,] we have

[MATH: \textrm E[a] = a.]

Therefore,

[MATH: \textrm E[1.2] = 1.2.]

---

Item 5 — Tutorial: The Expected Value of a Scaled Random Variable

Content:
We can also factor constants outside of an expected value expression. So for any constant [MATH: a] and any random variable [MATH: X,] we have

Content:
[MATH: \textrm E[aX] = a \textrm E[X].]

Content:
For example,

Content:
[MATH: \textrm E[5X] = 5 \textrm E[X],\qquad\textrm E[-9X] = -9 \textrm E[X], \qquad \textrm E[\pi X] = \pi \textrm E[X].]

Content:
We can prove this rule using the definition of the expected value, as follows:

Content:
[MATH: E[aX]|= ∑_(x ∈ S)ax ⋅ f(x); = a∑_(x ∈ S)x ⋅ f(x); = aE[X]]

---

Item 6 — Example: Computing the Expected Value of a Scaled Random Variable

Example Prompt:
A random variable [MATH: X] has the probability distribution given below.

| [MATH: x] | [MATH: 0] | [MATH: 1] | [MATH: 2] | [MATH: 3] | [MATH: 4] |
| [MATH: f(x)] | [MATH: \dfrac{1}{5}] | [MATH: \dfrac{1}{10}] | [MATH: \dfrac{3}{10}] | [MATH: \dfrac{3}{10}] | [MATH: \dfrac{1}{10}] |

Calculate [MATH: \textrm E\left[\dfrac{1}{4}X\right].]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
First, let's find [MATH: \textrm E[X].]

The expected value of a discrete random variable [MATH: X] with probability mass function [MATH: f(x)] and sample space [MATH: S] is given by

[MATH: \textrm E[X] = \sum\limits_{x \in S} x \cdot f(x).]

Summing up the products of each value of [MATH: X] and its associated probability, we get

[MATH: E[X]|= ∑_(x ∈ S)x ⋅ f(x); = 0 ⋅ (1)/(5) + 1 ⋅ (1)/(10) + 2 ⋅ (3)/(10) + 3 ⋅ (3)/(10) + 4 ⋅ (1)/(10); = 2.]

Therefore,

[MATH: E[(1)/(4)X]|= E[(1)/(4)X]; = (1)/(4)E[X]; = (1)/(4) ⋅ 2; = (1)/(2).]

Item 9 — Tutorial: The Expected Value of a Transformed Random Variable

Content:
Finally, we can combine the factor and constant rules into one simple rule.

Content:
Suppose that [MATH: X] is a random variable and [MATH: a] and [MATH: b] are constants. By combining our two rules, we have

Content:
[MATH: \textrm E[aX + b] = a\textrm E[X] + b.]

Content:
For example, if we know that [MATH: \textrm{E}[X] = 4,] then

Content:
[MATH: E[3X + 2]|= E[3X + 2]; = 3E[X] + 2; = 3(4) + 2; = 12 + 2; = 14.]

---

Item 10 — Example: Computing the Expected Value of a Transformed Random Variable

Example Prompt:

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
For any constants [MATH: a] and [MATH: b] and any random variable [MATH: X,] we have

[MATH: \textrm E[aX+b] = a \textrm E[X]+b.]

Therefore,

[MATH: E[1 − 4X]|= E[− 4X + 1]; = − 4E[X] + 1; = − 4((1)/(2)) + 1; = − 2 + 1; = − 1.]
